## 4 待确认事项与使用规则

1. 主统计期已批准保持2025.07–2026.06；外部文献更新截至本次检索日2026-11-04。是否将该日作为正式信息截止日，须用户评审确认。
2. S09和S10含主期之后的材料；以独立观察框或明确标注的后续趋势使用，禁止回填到主期统计。S12和S13用于历史及方法背景，避免以旧窗口说明2026年现状。
3. S13摘要明确为2020.06–2025.08，但附录数据来源表写2020.06–2025.07。该差异必须在使用其时间序列前追溯数据集与作者说明；目前不替作者裁定。
4. S13页面标注Preprint。其对开放权重与开源的操作性分类不能未经说明就成为本报告唯一法律或技术定义。
5. S04/S08的数值与图件需要回到旧仓库或具体数据表复核，不能因为已经排版成PDF就视为已验证。模拟材料不得作为经验结论证据。
6. S03/S06是可变在线页面；目前只有检索日期，不应称已完成全站冻结。后续需登记页面地址、获取时间、关联仓库commit与具体资产哈希。
7. S05/S07是流程与视觉参照，不应把专著中的研究结论不加区分地迁入GOSD；需保留原研究窗口、来源和适用条件。
8. 来源可读取与图表可复用不同。转载或改绘时保留作者、标题、来源链接、版本、图号与许可记录；尚未完成各外部图表的许可逐项核验。
9. 尚未独立下载并检查S13配套数据集、S09/S10全部图表底表，也未逐图核对S08视觉。它们是后续研究与样节工作中的明确检查项，不应写成已完成。

## 5 后续最小证据卡字段

每项拟写入正文的发现登记：主张编号、来源编号、对象/总体、指标定义、时间窗口、平台与地理口径、筛选与去重、数据/脚本版本、结果表、图号、原始或模拟标记、限制、核验人及核验状态。先有可追溯证据，再决定正文表述强度。

建议状态仅用：待核实、已读取、已复算、图文已验收、已批准使用。当前清单主要达到“已读取／版本已定位”，不是最后三个状态。

## 文件公开范围

本仓库只发布本轮规划与评审文字。三份输入 PDF、需求附件及生成的评审 PDF 均不入库；这里的文件名、页数和校验值用于识别内部评审依据，不代表存在公开下载入口。外部公开来源通过各自官方链接访问。

[返回评审入口](../README.md)

## 附录补充入口

- 附录A：[指标、数据与研究方法](https://www.x-lab.info/2026-Global-Open-Source-Development-Report/2026/zh/methodology/)。2026年11月4日已读取正文；沿用S02/S03的来源身份，不另计独立证据。
- 附录B：[模型开放条件与数字公共品研究参照](https://www.x-lab.info/2026-Global-Open-Source-Development-Report/2026/zh/appendices/dpg/)。2026年11月4日已读取页面及结构；同属S02/S03，未完成各外部规范和固定版本案例的重新核验。
- 两篇附录作为重构输入同步维护，职责、证据字段和样节联动见[附录规划](appendix-plan.md)。

附录编号核对：全书目录和dpg正文采用A方法/B模型开放；第六章菜单仍有A/B/C旧编号。declaration页面明确宣言来源已并入引言，故不得遗漏宣言内容，也不依据旧菜单重复建第三篇附录。[宣言来源入口](https://www.x-lab.info/2026-Global-Open-Source-Development-Report/2026/zh/appendices/declaration/)于2026年11月4日已读取。详见附录规划的编号沿革表。

L75: This post examines how the open source AI landscape has shifted across competition, geography, technical trends, and emerging communities over the past year. We primarily examine community activity on Hugging Face across many types of metrics to give a holistic view of the ecosystem.
L76: This post builds on an earlier analysis conducted mid-2025, 【42†available here】, which examined what the Hugging Face Community is building. We recommend reading additional perspectives on the open source ecosystem in and outside of Hugging Face from the 【43†Data Provenance Initiative†arxiv.org】, 【44†Interconnects†www.interconnects.ai】, 【45†OpenRouter and a16z†openrouter.ai】, and 【46†MIT and the Linux Foundation†www.linuxfoundation.org】.
L77: As the Hugging Face ecosystem is distributed, analyses are a combination of Hugging Face and community members' work, each of which is appropriately credited.
L78: Activity in the open source AI ecosystem has rapidly grown, with the number of users, model, and dataset repositories all close to doubling. In 2025, Hugging Face grew to 13 million users, more than 2 million public models, and over 500,000 public datasets.
L79: This growth signals more than increased interest in open source; it reflects a shift toward active participation, with users increasingly creating derivative artifacts such as fine-tuned models, adapters, benchmarks, and applications rather than only consuming pre-trained systems.
L80: Data from Hugging Face | Hugging Face's two million models and counting: 【47†Graph and story by AI World†aiworld.eu】
L81: 
L82: The ecosystem remains highly concentrated. Approximately half of the models on Hugging Face have less than 200 total downloads, and the top 200 most downloaded models, or 0.01% of models, comprise 49.6% of all downloads.
L83: Specialized communities form around particular domains, languages, or problem areas, and often show sustained engagement and reuse even when their overall download counts are modest. Open source AI is best understood as a collection of overlapping sub-ecosystems rather than a single uniform market.
L84: ## Open Source in Competition
L85: More companies, both large and small, are building on open source. Over 30% of the Fortune 500 now maintain verified accounts on Hugging Face. Startups frequently use open models as default components: 【48†Thinking Machines built its Tinker model options entirely on open weights,†thinkingmachines.ai】 while popular IDEs such as 【49†VSCode†code.visualstudio.com】 and 【50†Cursor†cursor.com】 support both open and closed models.
L86: 【51†Established American companies such as Airbnb have increased their engagement with the open ecosystem†www.thewirechina.com】, and Hugging Face has seen more 【5†legacy companies upgrading their organizational subscriptions】 over the course of 2025.
L87: Big Tech companies are frequently creating new repositories on Hugging Face Hub; visualized side-by-side, the strong increase in repository growth shows investment over time. NVIDIA has emerged as the strongest contributor.
L88: 
L89: Data from Hugging Face | Big Tech Is All-In On Open-Source AI, 【52†Graph and story by AI World†aiworld.eu】
L90: Studies of open software more broadly suggest that the downstream value created by open artifacts far exceeds the cost of producing them. Similar dynamics are emerging in AI, where open models are reused, adapted, and specialized across thousands of downstream applications. Organizations that rely exclusively on closed systems often incur higher costs and face reduced flexibility in deployment and customization.
L91: ## The Geography of Open Source
L92: 
L93: All-time downloads over the past four years show clear frontrunner regions in model popularity. The U.S. and China have historically been top contributors, with the UK, Germany, and France as secondary in popularity. Models developed by individual users or distributed organizations without a clear geographic base account for about half of all platform downloads.
L94: Data from Hugging Face | 【53†Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”†www.dataprovenance.org】
L95: 
L96: The geographic composition of the open source ecosystem has fundamentally changed. Hugging Face data shows China surpassing the U.S. in monthly downloads and overall downloads. In the past year, Chinese models quickly accounted for the plurality or 41% of downloads.
L97: 
L98: Data and Graph from Hugging Face
L99: Industry's share of overall development fell from around 70% before 2022 to roughly 37% in 2025. Meanwhile, independent or unaffiliated developers rose from 17% to 39% of all downloads over the same period, at times accounting for more than half of total usage. Individuals and small collectives focused on quantizing, adapting, and redistributing base models. These intermediaries now steer a meaningful portion of what typical users can run and how innovations spread through the ecosystem.
L100: Data from Hugging Face | 【53†Graph and Research from Longpre et al. “Economies of Open Intelligence: Tracing Power & Participation in the Model Ecosystem”†www.dataprovenance.org】
L101: Different regions contribute in different ways. The United States and Western Europe have historically dominated through large industry labs (Google, Meta, OpenAI, Stability AI), while China has increasingly led on both releases and adoption. France, Germany, and the UK continue to contribute through research organizations, national AI initiatives, and specialized model families. Ecosystems supporting a variety of contributors and organizational forms tend to produce more widely adopted artifacts.
L102: #### Countries, Organizations, and Individual Users
L103: 
L104: Popular models from startups were more widespread. Competitive countries were France and South Korea. Notably, the fourth most popular entity for developing new trending models were individual users, not organizations. Creating competitive models at a user level is more accessible than ever before.
L105: 
L106: Data and Graph from Hugging Face
L107: #### Between the U.S. and China
L108: Of the newly created models in 2025, the majority of trending models were either developed in China or derivative of a model developed in China. The most popular models were developed by large organizations, predominantly from the U.S. and China. For more on the Chinese AI ecosystem, read our three part series reflecting on the changes in one year since the "DeepSeek Moment", with one on 【54†strategic changes】, 【55†two on architectural changes】, 【56†and three on organizations and the future】.
L109: In 2025, China’s AI ecosystem steered heavily into open source, following the viral release of DeepSeek’s R1 model in January. The number of competitive Chinese organizations releasing models and the number of repositories on Hugging Face skyrocketed. Baidu went from zero releases on the Hub in 2024 to over 100 in 2025. ByteDance and Tencent each increased releases by eight to nine times.
L110: Organizations that had previously favored closed approaches, including Baidu and MiniMax, shifted decisively toward open releases.

L209: ## 1. Introduction
L210: We introduce our first-generation reasoning models, DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1. DeepSeek-R1-Zero, a model trained via large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) without supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a preliminary step, demonstrated remarkable performance on reasoning. With RL, DeepSeek-R1-Zero naturally emerged with numerous powerful and interesting reasoning behaviors. However, DeepSeek-R1-Zero encounters challenges such as endless repetition, poor readability, and language mixing.
L211: To address these issues and further enhance reasoning performance, we introduce DeepSeek-R1, which incorporates cold-start data before RL. DeepSeek-R1 achieves performance comparable to OpenAI-o1 across math, code, and reasoning tasks. To support the research community, we have open-sourced DeepSeek-R1-Zero, DeepSeek-R1, and six dense models distilled from DeepSeek-R1 based on Llama and Qwen.
L212: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B outperforms OpenAI-o1-mini across various benchmarks, achieving new state-of-the-art results for dense models.
L213: NOTE: Before running DeepSeek-R1 series models locally, we kindly recommend reviewing the 【62†Usage Recommendation】 section.

L216: ## 2. Model Summary
L217: 
L218: * * *
L219: 
L220: Post-Training: Large-Scale Reinforcement Learning on the Base Model
L221:   * We directly apply reinforcement learning (RL) to the base model without relying on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) as a preliminary step. This approach allows the model to explore chain-of-thought (CoT) for solving complex problems, resulting in the development of DeepSeek-R1-Zero. DeepSeek-R1-Zero demonstrates capabilities such as self-verification, reflection, and generating long CoTs, marking a significant milestone for the research community.
L222: Notably, it is the first open research to validate that reasoning capabilities of LLMs can be incentivized purely through RL, without the need for SFT. This breakthrough paves the way for future advancements in this area.
L223:   * We introduce our pipeline to develop DeepSeek-R1. The pipeline incorporates two RL stages aimed at discovering improved reasoning patterns and aligning with human preferences, as well as two SFT stages that serve as the seed for the model's reasoning and non-reasoning capabilities. We believe the pipeline will benefit the industry by creating better models.
L224: 
L225: * * *
L226: 
L227: Distillation: Smaller Models Can Be Powerful Too
L228:   * We demonstrate that the reasoning patterns of larger models can be distilled into smaller models, resulting in better performance compared to the reasoning patterns discovered through RL on small models. The open source DeepSeek-R1, as well as its API, will benefit the research community to distill better smaller models in the future.
L229:   * Using the reasoning data generated by DeepSeek-R1, we fine-tuned several dense models that are widely used in the research community. The evaluation results demonstrate that the distilled smaller dense models perform exceptionally well on benchmarks. We open-source distilled 1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B, 32B, and 70B checkpoints based on Qwen2.5 and Llama3 series to the community.

L95: If frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below shows a different story.

L104: Data from Hugging Face

L108: Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

L100: ## 2  Methodology
L101: ### 2.1  Data Sources and Collection
L102: We rely on a variety of data sources in this report. The primary data is composed of aggregated, public data on the open model platform Hugging Face, which measures downloads of each model and highlights model derivatives (i.e. which models are used as base models for fine-tuning).
L103: We also include data from public benchmarking websites Artificial Analysis (【40†Artificial Analysis, 2026】) and Arena (formerly ChatBotArena) (【39†Chiang et al., 2024】) to showcase model performance and other adoption data from the popular open model inference platform 【47†OpenRouter.ai†openrouter.ai】.
L104: #### Hugging Face Downloads.
L105: The primary adoption signal is cumulative download counts over time from the Hugging Face Hub, which is the primary destination for open models and provides publicly accessible data. By taking daily snapshots of the total downloads of every model, we can showcase trends of data not directly on 【48†huggingface.co†huggingface.co】.
L106: A “download” is defined as any HTTP request to the model file hosting endpoint, including programmatic access via transformers, curl, and similar tools^{2}^{2} 2 See the 【49†Hugging Face documentation†huggingface.co】 for more details. We obtained historical monthly download data directly from the Hugging Face team for the leading open model organizations – Meta Llama, Qwen, Mistral AI, DeepSeek, Google, and Microsoft – covering November 2023 through July 10, 2025.
L107: Beginning in early July 2025, we operate an independent daily scraper that records total cumulative downloads and other public metadata for all publicly available models. The historical series (through July 10, 2025) uses $2.5\times$ IQR outlier-filtered data (described below). From August 2025 onward, we compute monthly deltas from the unfiltered scraper data and add them to the filtered baseline, preserving continuity at the splice point without re-filtering the full history.
L108: Throughout, monthly labels refer to data as of the first of that month: “Aug 25” denotes cumulative downloads through July 31, 2025.
L109: Throughout the report we refer to open models, open language models, and open-weight language models. The final term is the most precise, as we are measuring the adoption of any set of model weights available on the Hugging Face platform, regardless of license or information available about it (which could earn it the classification “open-source”).
L110: We track every prominent open language model released since ChatGPT – i.e. models that accept text (and optionally other modalities) as input and produce text as output – while excluding embedding models, text-to-image diffusion models, and other non-generative architectures.
L111: The full list of $\sim$1.5K tracked models is publicly available.^{3}^{3} 3 【50†https://github.com/Interconnects-AI/tracked-models/blob/main/models.csv†github.com】 In total, these models account for over 3 billion downloads across the study period (November 2023 through March 2026). To mitigate noise on the initial data, we applied $2.5\times$ interquartile range outlier detection on daily download series; models without anomalous spikes are left unfiltered.
L112: This substantially improved the historical data, which is prone to large variations and unexplainable features.
L113: For derivative and fine-tune tracking, we identify derivatives via the Hugging Face base_model tag, which records the parent model in the format base_model:ORG/MODEL. We restrict to derivatives whose base model appears in our tracked model list, require more than five lifetime downloads, and exclude local-inference re-uploads (e.g., GGUF, MLX).
L114: #### OpenRouter.
L115: 
L116: Inference token share data is drawn from OpenRouter, which provided historical data on the top 10 open models per month ranked by total tokens served. Only the top 10 are reported for each month, so organizations whose usage is spread across time or many models may be undercounted. This provides a complementary demand signal, capturing which models people use, which is not reflected in download counts alone.
L117: #### Arena.
L118: Aside from quantitative metrics, we also take into account qualitative metrics to showcase the progress of open models. Community Elo ratings come from Arena (formerly ChatBotArena), which measures general chat quality through blind pairwise comparisons by human evaluators (【39†Chiang et al., 2024】). We use the style-controlled overall Elo as the primary performance metric.
